q: A project specifies a very efficient chiller (0.45 kW/ton) but pairs it with a poorly controlled cooling tower. What is the LEED implication?

The efficient chiller compensates for the poor cooling tower
This would earn extra LEED points for the efficient chiller
Cooling tower efficiency does not affect chiller performance
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EA concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: cooling tower: heat-rejection equipment that commonly uses evaporation; energy and atmosphere: strategies addressing energy demand, efficiency, refrigerants, and renewable energy; energy efficiency: delivery of the required service with less energy use
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: System efficiency depends on both — chiller plant must be optimized as an integrated system.
logic: The chiller plant is a system. A high-efficiency chiller (0.45 kW/ton rated) rejecting heat into poorly controlled condenser water (high temperatures from inadequate cooling tower performance) operates far below rated kW/ton. System thinking — chiller, cooling tower, condenser water pump, and controls together — is the correct approach.

q: A rainwater collection system has a 20,000-gallon cistern but no submetering. What LEED limitation does this create?

Submetering is only required for cooling tower systems
No limitation — the system earns WE credit regardless of metering

vocabulary: cooling tower: heat-rejection equipment that commonly uses evaporation; submetering: separate measurement of water or energy use by system or end use; credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Without submetering, alternative water delivery cannot be verified for LEED credits.
logic: Submetering alternative water systems serves two purposes: documenting the actual volume used (supporting WE credit claims) and enabling ongoing performance verification for LEED O+M. q: An owner skips pre-design charette and jumps straight to schematic design. Six months later the team discovers a 15-degree rotation would have improved solar performance by 20%. What does this illustrate?

The mechanical engineer should have identified this independently
Charettes are a waste of time since the building was built anyway
The cost of optimization rises exponentially as design progresses

keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: The cost of optimization rises exponentially as design progresses.
logic: This illustrates the MacLeamy curve: the ability to influence cost and performance is highest in early design stages. A pre-design charette costing a few thousand dollars could have identified and implemented the rotation at near-zero cost. q: A project proposes eliminating mechanical ventilation on mild days and relying entirely on operable windows. What LEED IAQ concern does this raise?

Operable windows eliminate all LEED IAQ requirements

keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Natural ventilation must demonstrate adequate outdoor air across all conditions.

logic: One of the most-cited barriers to transit use is 'what if I need to leave unexpectedly?'
